_meta.description: Curated, paraphrased seed knowledge base of MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise techniques relevant to network-traffic-visible behaviour, grouped under this project's five simplified kill-chain stages. Descriptions are written in our own words for retrieval/summarization purposes, not copied from attack.mitre.org. Technique IDs and tactic names are factual references. For production use, regenerate this file from the official STIX corpus (github.com/mitre-attack/attack-stix-data) with scripts/sync_attck.py (see knowledge_base.py) to get full coverage and stay current.
_meta.source: MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise, curated subset, manually verified technique IDs

entries.name: Active Scanning
entries.summary: An adversary probes a target's IP ranges or services directly, e.g. port sweeps or vulnerability scans, to map what is reachable before choosing an attack path.
entries.network_signature: Many distinct destination ports/hosts contacted from one source in a short window, often with a high SYN-to-SYN-ACK ratio (half-open connections).
entries.mitigation: Rate-limit and alert on connection fan-out per source IP; deploy network intrusion prevention tuned to scan signatures; minimize exposed service surface.

entries.name: Gather Victim Host Information
entries.summary: Passive or semi-passive collection of details about specific hosts (OS, software, hardware) to plan a later exploit.
entries.network_signature: Often invisible on the wire (OSINT-based); when active, shows as banner-grabbing connections to service ports.
entries.mitigation: Limit public exposure of host/service banners; monitor for banner-grab patterns (connect-then-immediately-disconnect).

entries.name: Gather Victim Network Information
entries.summary: Collection of network topology, IP ranges, and domain data, frequently via DNS enumeration or WHOIS lookups, to plan targeting.
entries.network_signature: Bursts of DNS queries for sequential or dictionary-style subdomains from a single resolver.
entries.mitigation: Monitor DNS query volume/entropy per client; consider split-horizon DNS to limit externally visible topology.

entries.name: Network Service Discovery
entries.summary: Once inside a network (or from outside), the adversary enumerates which services are running on which hosts, commonly with tools like Nmap.
entries.network_signature: Sequential or randomized destination-port sweeps against one or many internal hosts; low payload size per packet.
entries.mitigation: Internal network segmentation; host-based firewall rules that alert on unexpected inbound probes between segments.

entries.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
entries.summary: The adversary exploits a vulnerability in an internet-facing application (web server, API, VPN gateway) to gain an initial foothold.
entries.network_signature: Malformed or unusually long requests to a public service, often followed by an outbound connection from that service shortly after (exploitation -> callback).
entries.mitigation: Patch internet-facing software promptly; deploy a WAF; monitor for anomalous outbound connections initiated by server-tier hosts.

entries.name: Valid Accounts
entries.attck_tactic: Initial Access / Persistence / Privilege Escalation / Defense Evasion
entries.summary: The adversary authenticates using legitimate, often stolen or brute-forced, credentials rather than exploiting a software flaw — making the activity look like normal user behaviour.
entries.network_signature: A burst of authentication attempts (high SYN/ACK handshake ratio to an auth service) possibly followed by login from an unusual source IP or at an unusual hour.
entries.mitigation: MFA on all remote-access and admin accounts; rate-limit and lock out repeated authentication failures; alert on impossible-travel or new-device logins.

entries.name: Brute Force
entries.summary: Systematic guessing of credentials against an authentication service, either exhaustively or via a curated password list.
entries.network_signature: High-frequency, low-payload connection attempts to a single authentication port from one source, dominated by SYN and immediate RST/FIN.
entries.mitigation: Account lockout / exponential backoff after failed attempts; CAPTCHA on public login forms; monitor and alert on failure-rate spikes.

entries.name: External Remote Services
entries.summary: Abuse of legitimate remote-access services (VPN, RDP gateway, SSH) exposed to the internet to gain entry.
entries.network_signature: Inbound connections to remote-access ports from geographies or ASNs with no prior history for that account/service.
entries.mitigation: Restrict remote-access exposure to known IP ranges where feasible; enforce MFA; log and alert on first-seen source ASN for privileged services.

entries.name: Remote Services
entries.summary: The adversary uses standard remote-access protocols already present in the environment (RDP, SMB/Windows admin shares, SSH) to move from one internal host to another.
entries.network_signature: Internal host-to-host connections on 3389/445/22 outside that host's normal peer set, often with sustained byte volume characteristic of file or session transfer.
entries.mitigation: Segment the network so lateral RDP/SMB/SSH is denied by default between workstation subnets; require jump-hosts for admin protocols; log and baseline internal east-west traffic.

entries.name: Lateral Tool Transfer
entries.summary: Copying attacker tools or malware from one compromised host to another inside the network to extend the foothold.
entries.network_signature: Internal transfer of an executable-sized payload over SMB or a file-sharing protocol between hosts that don't normally exchange files.
entries.mitigation: Application allow-listing on endpoints; alert on binary/script transfer over internal file shares to workstations.

entries.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material
entries.attck_tactic: Lateral Movement / Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation
entries.summary: The adversary reuses stolen session tokens, hashes, or Kerberos tickets to authenticate as another user without knowing their password (e.g. pass-the-hash).
entries.network_signature: Authentication events that skip the normal password-exchange pattern, often followed immediately by privileged actions from a host that did not previously use that account.
entries.mitigation: Credential Guard / hash isolation on endpoints; short-lived Kerberos ticket lifetimes; alert on the same credential authenticating from multiple hosts in a short window.

entries.name: Application Layer Protocol
entries.summary: The implant communicates with its controller using an ordinary application protocol (HTTP/S, DNS) so the traffic blends in with legitimate use.
entries.network_signature: Low-volume, highly periodic (low inter-arrival-time variance) requests to a small set of external destinations, often with unusually consistent payload sizes — a beacon pattern.
entries.mitigation: TLS-inspecting proxy with domain reputation filtering; detect beacon periodicity via jitter analysis on outbound flows; block/alert on rare or newly-registered destination domains.

entries.name: Ingress Tool Transfer
entries.summary: The adversary downloads additional tools or malware onto the compromised host from external infrastructure.
entries.network_signature: An outbound connection followed by an inbound payload of executable-like size shortly after initial compromise indicators.
entries.mitigation: Egress filtering / allow-listed outbound destinations for server-tier hosts; endpoint detection on newly-written executables correlated with a recent network transfer.

entries.name: Proxy
entries.summary: Traffic is relayed through an intermediary (internal or external proxy, or a compromised third party) to obscure the true C2 destination.
entries.network_signature: Repeated connections to a single internal host that itself fans out to varying external destinations — an internal host acting as an unexpected relay.
entries.mitigation: Restrict which hosts may act as egress points; monitor for internal hosts whose outbound destination diversity suddenly increases.

entries.name: Encrypted Channel
entries.summary: C2 traffic is wrapped in encryption beyond what the carrier protocol provides, to defeat content inspection.
entries.network_signature: TLS sessions with non-standard certificate characteristics or JA3/JA3S fingerprints inconsistent with the claimed client software, on a periodic beacon cadence.
entries.mitigation: TLS fingerprinting (JA3/JA3S) against known-good baselines; certificate transparency monitoring for lookalike domains.

entries.name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
entries.summary: Stolen data is sent out through the same channel already used for command and control, avoiding a second, more detectable connection.
entries.network_signature: A sustained increase in outbound byte volume on an already-established beacon connection, breaking its previously steady, small payload pattern.
entries.mitigation: Baseline per-connection byte volume and alert on deviation; data-loss-prevention inspection on egress even for 'known' C2-looking flows.

entries.name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol
entries.summary: Data leaves the network over a protocol different from the one used for C2 — e.g. DNS tunneling or FTP — often chosen because it is less scrutinized.
entries.network_signature: Unusually large or frequent DNS TXT/NULL queries, or outbound FTP/SFTP sessions to destinations with no legitimate business relationship.
entries.mitigation: Restrict outbound DNS to approved resolvers; monitor DNS query/response size distributions; egress-filter uncommon exfiltration-capable protocols by default.

entries.name: Exfiltration Over Web Service
entries.summary: Stolen data is uploaded to a legitimate cloud storage or collaboration service to blend in with sanctioned SaaS traffic.
entries.network_signature: Large outbound uploads to consumer cloud-storage endpoints from hosts/accounts with no business reason to use that service.
entries.mitigation: CASB / SaaS-aware egress policy restricting upload to sanctioned tenants only; DLP scanning on outbound web uploads.

entries.name: Data Transfer Size Limits
entries.summary: The adversary caps individual transfer sizes and spreads exfiltration across many small transfers to stay under volume-based detection thresholds.
entries.network_signature: Many small, evenly-sized outbound transfers spread over a long window rather than one large burst — low single-flow volume, high cumulative volume.
entries.mitigation: Track cumulative outbound volume per host/account over rolling windows, not just per-flow; alert on sustained low-and-slow transfer patterns.
